q: Sec-butyl alcohol, CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃, should be named by IUPAC rules as:
x: The longest chain has four carbons and is numbered from the end nearer the –OH, putting it on C-2. 'Butan-3-ol' numbers from the wrong end.

q: Which of the following is a primary alcohol?
x: In (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH (2-methylpropan-1-ol) the –OH carbon is joined to only one other carbon, so it is primary. (CH₃)₂CHOH and butan-2-ol are secondary; (CH₃)₃COH is tertiary.

q: The general formula of saturated monohydric alcohols is:
x: A saturated monohydric alcohol is an alkane with one H replaced by –OH, so it is CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH (for example C₂H₅OH when n = 2).

q: Allyl alcohol, CH₂=CHCH₂OH, is called in the IUPAC system:
x: The –OH group gets the lowest number, so the carbon carrying it is C-1 and the double bond starts at C-2: prop-2-en-1-ol. 'Prop-1-en-3-ol' numbers from the wrong end.

q: Structurally, an alcohol can be regarded as a derivative of water in which:
o: Both hydrogen atoms are replaced by alkyl groups
One hydrogen atom is replaced by an alkyl group
The oxygen atom is replaced by a carbon atom
One hydrogen atom is replaced by a phenyl ring
x: Replacing one H of H–O–H by an alkyl group gives R–O–H, an alcohol. Replacing both gives an ether, R–O–R′; replacing one by a benzene ring gives a phenol.

q: Which of the isomeric butyl alcohols (C₄H₉OH) has the lowest boiling point?
x: All four form hydrogen bonds, but branching makes the molecule more compact, reducing surface contact and van der Waals forces. The most branched isomer, 2-methylpropan-2-ol, boils lowest; the straight-chain butan-1-ol boils highest.

q: Ethanol, C₂H₅OH, and methoxymethane, CH₃OCH₃, have the same molecular formula, but ethanol has a much higher boiling point. This is because:
o: Methoxymethane has a larger molar mass
Ethanol has an O–H bond, so its molecules hydrogen-bond to one another
Methoxymethane molecules form stronger hydrogen bonds
x: The two are functional isomers with equal molar masses. Only ethanol has a hydrogen on oxygen, so only ethanol molecules hydrogen-bond to each other; the ether has only weaker dipole forces.

q: Which of the following is a secondary alcohol?
x: In cyclohexanol the carbon bearing –OH is bonded to two ring carbons, so it is secondary. Benzyl alcohol and ethanol are primary; 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary.

q: Ethanol is heated with excess concentrated sulphuric acid at about 170 °C. The main organic product is:
x: At about 170 °C with excess acid, ethanol is dehydrated (loses H₂O within one molecule) to give ethene. At a lower temperature with excess ethanol, the ether is formed instead.

q: Ethanol is warmed with sodium bromide and concentrated sulphuric acid, which together produce HBr. The organic product is:
x: HBr substitutes Br for the –OH group: C₂H₅OH + HBr → C₂H₅Br + H₂O. 1,2-Dibromoethane would need Br₂ adding across ethene.

q: The correct order of reactivity of alcohols towards Lucas reagent (forming alkyl chlorides) is:
x: The C–O bond breaks most easily in tertiary alcohols, which give cloudiness at once; secondary ones take a few minutes and primary ones react only on heating.

q: The rate of reaction of alcohols with metallic sodium, in which the O–H bond breaks, follows the order:
o: All three react at the same rate
x: Alkyl groups push electrons towards oxygen, making the O–H hydrogen harder to remove. A tertiary alcohol has the most alkyl groups, so it reacts most slowly with sodium; this is the reverse of the Lucas test order.

q: Ethanol reacts with phosphorus trichloride: 3C₂H₅OH + PCl₃ → 3C₂H₅Cl + ?. The other product is:
x: With PCl₃ the by-product is phosphorous acid, H₃PO₃. POCl₃ and HCl are the by-products when PCl₅ is used instead.

q: When an alcohol is dehydrated by concentrated H₂SO₄, the first step is:
o: Protonation of the oxygen of the –OH group by H⁺
Loss of a hydride ion from the –OH carbon
Attack of HSO₄⁻ on the oxygen atom
Removal of the O–H hydrogen as H⁺ by the acid
x: The acid protonates the –OH oxygen, turning it into –OH₂⁺, which leaves as a water molecule, a far better leaving group than OH⁻. Here the alcohol acts as a base, not an acid.

q: 0.4 mol of ethane-1,2-diol, HOCH₂CH₂OH, reacts completely with excess sodium. What volume of hydrogen forms at STP? (1 mol gas = 22.4 dm³)
x: Each molecule has two –OH groups, and 2 –OH give 1 H₂, so 1 mol diol gives 1 mol H₂. 0.4 mol H₂ × 22.4 = 8.96 dm³. 4.48 dm³ counts only one –OH group.

q: Propan-1-ol is warmed with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ and the product is distilled off as soon as it forms. The product is:
x: A primary alcohol is first oxidised to an aldehyde; removing it at once stops further oxidation to propanoic acid. Propanone would come from the secondary alcohol, propan-2-ol.

q: Ethanol is heated with concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 140 °C, with the alcohol in excess. The main organic product is:
x: At about 140 °C with excess ethanol, two molecules lose one water molecule between them: 2C₂H₅OH → C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + H₂O. At about 170 °C with excess acid, ethene forms instead.

q: Propanoic acid is heated with ethanol and a little concentrated H₂SO₄. The structure of the ester formed is:
x: The acid part (CH₃CH₂CO–) joins to the alkyl part of the alcohol through oxygen, giving ethyl propanoate, CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₃. CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃ is its isomer, propyl ethanoate.

q: Which pair of compounds reacts in the presence of concentrated H₂SO₄ to give ethyl methanoate, HCOOC₂H₅?
x: In an ester name, the alkyl group ('ethyl') comes from the alcohol and the '-oate' part from the acid ('methanoate'), so the reactants are methanoic acid and ethanol. Ethanoic acid with methanol gives the isomer methyl ethanoate.

q: Besides the ester, the other product of the reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol is:
x: Acid + alcohol ⇌ ester + water. Hydrogen chloride is produced only when an acid chloride is used in place of the carboxylic acid.

q: The esterification of ethanol with ethanoic acid is reversible. The yield of ethyl ethanoate can be increased by:
o: Using dilute instead of concentrated H₂SO₄
x: Adding excess of a reactant shifts the equilibrium towards the products. Adding water pushes it back towards the reactants, and a catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium at all.

q: In the Williamson synthesis of ethers, an alkyl halide is treated with sodium alkoxide. The alkoxide ion acts as:
o: An electrophile that attacks the halogen
A nucleophile that replaces the halogen
A dehydrating agent that removes water
x: The alkoxide ion, RO⁻, has a negative oxygen with lone pairs, so it attacks the carbon of the alkyl halide and displaces the halide ion in a nucleophilic substitution, giving R–O–R′.

q: The IUPAC name of the ether CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₂CH₃ is:
x: Ethers are named as alkoxyalkanes, with the larger alkyl group as the parent chain: propane carrying an ethoxy group on C-1. 'Propoxyethane' wrongly makes the smaller group the parent.

q: An ester, CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃, was made by heating a carboxylic acid with an alcohol and a little concentrated H₂SO₄. The acid and alcohol used were:
x: CH₃CO– comes from ethanoic acid and –OCH₂CH₂CH₃ from propan-1-ol (propyl ethanoate). Propan-2-ol would give CH₃COOCH(CH₃)₂, and propanoic acid with ethanol gives the isomer CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₃.

q: The IUPAC name of the dihydric phenol C₆H₄(OH)₂ with the two –OH groups on neighbouring carbon atoms (catechol) is:
x: Neighbouring (ortho) positions are 1 and 2, so catechol is benzene-1,2-diol. Benzene-1,3-diol is resorcinol and benzene-1,4-diol is quinol (hydroquinone).

q: Carbon dioxide is bubbled through an aqueous solution of sodium phenoxide. What happens?
o: Nothing, because phenol is a stronger acid than carbonic acid
Sodium phenoxide is oxidised to benzoic acid
Phenol is converted into sodium benzoate
Phenol is set free, because carbonic acid is a stronger acid than phenol
x: Phenol is a weaker acid than carbonic acid, so CO₂ and water displace it: C₆H₅ONa + CO₂ + H₂O → C₆H₅OH + NaHCO₃. This is also why phenol does not liberate CO₂ from NaHCO₃.

q: Phenol reacts with metallic sodium to give:
x: 2C₆H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₆H₅ONa + H₂. Water is the by-product only when phenol reacts with NaOH, not with sodium metal.

q: Which of the following is a weaker acid than phenol?
x: The –CH₃ group releases electrons, destabilising the phenoxide ion, so 4-methylphenol (p-cresol) is less acidic than phenol. Nitro groups withdraw electrons and make phenols more acidic.

q: In the phenol molecule, a lone pair of electrons on the oxygen atom is:
o: Completely localised on the oxygen atom
Used to form a coordinate bond with hydrogen
Transferred to the ring as a hydride ion
Partly delocalised into the π electron system of the benzene ring
x: Overlap of an oxygen lone pair with the ring π system spreads electron density into the ring. This makes the ring more reactive and strengthens the C–O bond.

q: Phenol is only moderately soluble in cold water. Which statement best explains this?
o: It reacts with water to form phenoxide ions completely
It has no polar bonds, so it cannot interact with water
Its –OH group hydrogen-bonds with water, but the large C₆H₅ group is non-polar
It forms ionic bonds with water molecules
x: The –OH group can hydrogen-bond to water, giving some solubility, while the bulky hydrophobic benzene ring limits it. Phenol is only a weak acid, so very little ionises.

q: Phenol vapour is passed over heated zinc dust. The organic product is:
x: Zinc dust removes the oxygen: C₆H₅OH + Zn → C₆H₆ + ZnO. This reduction converts phenol back into benzene.

q: Phenol is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid at about 100 °C. The main product is:
x: Sulphonation of phenol gives mainly the ortho isomer at room temperature but the para isomer, 4-hydroxybenzenesulphonic acid, at about 100 °C. The meta isomer is not a main product because –OH directs ortho/para.

q: Compared with benzene, phenol undergoes electrophilic substitution:
o: Only in the presence of a strong Lewis acid
x: The –OH group feeds electron density into the ring, activating it, so phenol reacts with electrophiles far more readily than benzene, often without a catalyst.

q: When bromine water converts one mole of phenol fully into its white tribromo product, the inorganic by-product formed is:
x: C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃OH + 3HBr. Each substitution replaces one ring H by Br, and that H leaves with the other Br atom as HBr, so 3 mol HBr form.

q: The mixture of 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol from nitration of phenol can be separated by steam distillation, because 2-nitrophenol:
o: Has intramolecular hydrogen bonding, so it is more volatile
Has intermolecular hydrogen bonding, so it is less volatile
Has a much larger molar mass
x: In 2-nitrophenol the –OH and –NO₂ are close enough to hydrogen-bond within the molecule, so it does not associate with its neighbours and distils with steam. 4-Nitrophenol hydrogen-bonds between molecules and stays behind. The two have equal molar masses.

q: Nitration of phenol with dilute nitric acid gives very little of which isomer?
x: The –OH group directs the NO₂ group to the ortho (2-) and para (4-) positions, so the meta isomer, 3-nitrophenol, is formed in only a very small amount.

q: Which statement about the nitration of phenol and of benzene is correct?
o: Phenol is nitrated by dilute HNO₃ at room temperature; benzene needs concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄
Both need a mixture of concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ at 55 °C
Benzene is nitrated by dilute HNO₃; phenol needs concentrated acids
Neither can be nitrated without a FeCl₃ catalyst
x: The activated ring of phenol reacts even with dilute nitric acid in the cold. Benzene needs the nitrating mixture of concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids to produce enough NO₂⁺.

q: For electrophilic substitution on the benzene ring, the –OH group of phenol is classified as:
x: The –OH group donates electron density to the ring, increasing the rate (activating), and the extra density builds up at the ortho and para positions, so it directs there.

q: Ethanol forms an ester when heated with ethanoic acid and concentrated H₂SO₄, but phenol does not do so readily. To make phenyl ethanoate from phenol, a chemist would use:
x: Phenol is a poor nucleophile because its oxygen lone pair is delocalised into the ring, so the slow acid-catalysed esterification is not used. The more reactive acid chloride gives the ester: C₆H₅OH + CH₃COCl → CH₃COOC₆H₅ + HCl.

q: Which reagent can be used to distinguish phenol from cyclohexanol?
x: Phenol decolourises bromine water at once and gives a white precipitate because its ring is activated; cyclohexanol, a saturated alcohol, gives neither. Both give hydrogen with sodium.

q: When burnt in air, phenol and ethanol differ in that:
o: Ethanol burns with a sooty flame, while phenol does not burn
Phenol burns with a smoky (sooty) flame, while ethanol burns with a clean blue flame
Both burn with a clean blue flame
Phenol burns with a clean flame, while ethanol gives soot
x: Phenol is aromatic with a high carbon-to-hydrogen ratio, so combustion is incomplete and the flame is smoky. Ethanol burns almost completely with a pale blue flame.

q: X dissolves in aqueous NaOH but gives no gas with NaHCO₃ solution. Y does not dissolve in aqueous NaOH but gives hydrogen with sodium. X and Y could be:
x: Phenol is acidic enough to react with NaOH but too weak to release CO₂ from NaHCO₃, which fits X; ethanoic acid would give CO₂. Ethanol reacts with sodium but not with aqueous NaOH, which fits Y.

q: Benzyl alcohol, C₆H₅CH₂OH, contains a benzene ring and an –OH group, yet it is classed as an alcohol and not a phenol because:
o: The –OH is on an sp³ carbon of the side chain, not directly on the ring
Its –OH group is attached directly to the ring
It is more acidic than phenol
x: A phenol has –OH bonded directly to an aromatic ring carbon. In benzyl alcohol the –OH is on the CH₂ carbon, so it behaves as a primary alcohol and is less acidic than phenol.

q: In water, ethanol is neutral, while phenol is:
x: Phenol ionises slightly to give phenoxide and H⁺, so it is a weak acid (carbolic acid). Ethanol ionises even less than water and is regarded as neutral.

q: Which of the following dissolves in aqueous sodium hydroxide by forming a salt?
x: 2-Methylphenol (o-cresol) is a phenol, acidic enough to react with NaOH to form a sodium phenoxide salt. Cyclohexanol, benzyl alcohol and ethanol are alcohols and do not react with aqueous NaOH.
